question: In February 2024, the Commission’s Directorate-General for Maritime Affairs and Fisheries argued for new, longer closures, like the closure introduced by the French authorities following a court ruling, to avoid incidental catches of dolphins in the Bay of Biscay.

The announcement ignores the sector’s criticisms about how the measure has been adopted: with no impact studies, failing to meet the obligation to consult the regional councils and no immediate compensation mechanisms for ceasing activity.

The sector also criticises the decision as it ignores scientific reports funded by the Commission itself showing that the ultrasound devices tested avoid 90 % of incidents or imposes a general restriction regardless of the affected vessels’ history with this issue. In view of the above: 1.
What dialogue has the Commission established with the sector to respond to these criticisms?
Does the Commission consider it reasonable to introduce longer closures without trying other solutions devised together with the sector?
Does the Commission believe this action is in line with the common fisheries policy’s triple sustainability principle?
answer: 1. The Commission is in contact with the sector through the South-Western Waters Advisory Council and has provided several replies to the sector in the last three years. The Commission has regularly recalled that action is needed to reduce the incidental by-catches of common dolphins in the Bay of Biscay in accordance with the advice of the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) (1).

The Commission stressed the same in the EU Action Plan (2) in 2023. 2. The Commission has consistently reiterated over the years that mitigation measures do not only include spatio-temporal closures but that it welcomes projects on acoustic deterrent devices or other technical mitigation measures. The Commission follows the best scientific advice available, which is the ICES advice of 29 June 2023 (3).

In its advice, ICES reiterates that temporal closures in Subarea 8 in métiers of concern are likely to be the most effective management measures for reducing bycatch mortality in the short term”. 3. Article 11 of Regulation (EU) No 2019/1241 (4) and Article 12 of Directive 92/43/EEC (5) expressly prohibit catching cetaceans.

The Commission encourages Member States (6) to come up with measures, which can also be technical solutions, to put in place for winter 2024/2025, via a new joint recommendation. The Commission will ask the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF) to assess the recommendation, including its socioeconomic impact.
If the STECF assessment is positive on the measures and their impact to reduce by-catches of dolphins, the Commission will adopt a delegated act under Article 15 of Regulation (EU) No 2019/1241.
